name: Carry out preventive and corrective maintenance on gas units
summary: Plant maintenance keeps the converted gas steam units and cogeneration plants available between major outages. Preventive maintenance orders come out of the ERP plan each night and corrective requests come from operators; planners scope the job, reserve parts and schedule it weekly with operations, then millwrights or instrument and electrical technicians lock on under a permit, do the work and hand the equipment back for a test. Work is slowed by parts that are not in stock, by jobs that must wait for a unit outage, by the permit queue in outage seasons, and by poor completion notes that weaken the equipment history.

baseline.org_archetype: An Alberta merchant generator with three 400 to 460 MW coal units converted to gas in 2021 and two cogeneration plants, maintained by an in-house unionised craft workforce with an ERP plant maintenance module.
baseline.notes: Keephills 2 and 3 and Sundance 6 burned coal in 2019-2020 and gas from 2021, so work order volume fell during the period as coal handling, pulverisers and ash systems left service. Major outages are a separate process (eng-execute-major-outage).

trigger: A preventive maintenance order falls due in the ERP maintenance plan, or an operator raises a notification for a defect.
end_state: The work order is technically complete in the ERP with notes and failure codes, or the notification is cancelled as a duplicate.

volume.seasonality: Higher in April to June and September to November, when minor outages open outage-dependent backlog; lower in winter peak months when units are kept running.

surge.cause: spring and fall planned outage seasons

evidence.note: Outage seasons in spring and fall; the multiplier is lower than the organisation file's because major outage work orders belong to eng-execute-major-outage. Estimate.

The organisation file's mode of 2,000 orders a month needs about 75 to 90 craft FTE at 4 to 5 hands-on craft hours per order, but the file lists 60 plant crafts (34 millwrights, 26 technicians) who also work outages. 1,400 a month matches the craft headcount; the range keeps the coal years (higher) and gas years (lower). Estimate.

Org file lists 12 planners (gas-tech) for about 60 plant crafts, a 1:5 ratio; Palmer's base recommendation is 1:20 to 1:30 but he notes 1:5 to 1:15 still pays where planners also support outages and projects. At the minutes in this file all 12 are needed, because planners here also key completion data that a clerk could enter.
Org file lists 8 supervisors; about half their time goes to screening, scheduling, permits and close-out for routine orders, the rest to outages, safety and people management.
Org file lists 34 millwrights; the rest of their time is outage work, permit sign-on counted in the permit workflow, training and leave.
Org file lists 26 technicians; many also support DCS changes, outages, CEMS and calibration routes.

roles.title: Field operator (third- or fourth-class power engineer)

evidence.note: Post-maintenance testing share of the 55 field operators' time; estimate.

systems.name: ERP (finance, purchasing and plant maintenance modules)
Document management and engineering drawings repository

steps.name: Call PM order or receive notification
steps.description: Each night the ERP maintenance scheduling run calls preventive maintenance orders that fall due from the maintenance plans, with task list and parts list attached. Corrective work arrives instead as a notification raised by operators on shift. This step only routes the case.

next.condition: preventive maintenance order with standard task list
corrective notification from operations or inspection

evidence.note: Share of PM versus corrective orders estimated for a thermal plant in 2019-2022; Palmer (palmer) notes good plants still carry a fair amount of reactive work.

steps.name: Screen notification at morning meeting
steps.description: At the daily work-screening meeting the maintenance supervisor reads each new notification with the shift supervisor, checks it is not a duplicate, confirms the equipment and sets a priority from one (emergency) to four. Urgent jobs go straight to a crew; duplicates and non-jobs are closed.

error.defect_description: Priority set too low or too high, so the job is scheduled in the wrong week.

next.condition: priority 1 break-in job sent straight to a crew

evidence.note: Daily screening meeting is common practice in Alberta thermal plants; meeting held on weekday mornings by an office-hours supervisor, so notifications raised on Friday night wait for Monday.

steps.name: Convert notification to work order
steps.description: The planner opens the accepted notification in the ERP, creates a work order against the functional location, sets the work centre (mechanical or instrument and electrical), the priority date and the cost centre, and decides whether the job needs a walk-down before it can be planned.

error.defect_description: Order raised against the wrong functional location or work centre.

next.condition: job can be planned from history

evidence.note: Estimate based on common ERP plant maintenance practice (notification to order).

steps.name: Walk down the job in the plant
steps.description: The planner walks to the equipment, often with the operator who raised the problem, looks at access, scaffolding needs, isolation points and the condition of the part, takes photos and nameplate details, and notes any special tools or lifting needed.

error.defect_description: Access or lifting need missed during the walk-down.

evidence.note: Palmer describes planners preparing job plans in advance so crafts are not delayed; walk-down share and minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write the job plan
steps.description: The planner writes the job steps, crafts and hours, special tools, scaffolding and lifting needs, and the isolation points and hazards for the permit, copying from earlier orders on the same equipment where they exist. The plan is attached to the work order in the ERP.

error.defect_description: Job plan misses a part, a tool or an isolation point.

evidence.note: Planning function as described by Palmer; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Check stock and reserve parts
steps.description: The planner looks up each part on the bill of materials or by catalogue number in the ERP, checks stock on hand and open orders, and creates reservations against the work order. Non-stock or short parts go to purchasing.
inputs: job plan or PM task list

error.defect_description: Wrong part number reserved because of a poor catalogue description.

next.condition: all parts in stock and reserved

evidence.note: Reliabilityweb reports only 50 to 70 percent of planned work orders filled from stores in typical MRO storerooms; a generator with critical spares and PM kits is assumed to do better, so 26 percent of orders need a purchase (author's estimate).

steps.name: Raise purchase requisition
steps.description: The planner creates a purchase requisition in the ERP for each non-stock or short item, with the part number, supplier if known, required date and the work order as the account. The requisition goes to purchasing for approval and sourcing.

error.defect_description: Requisition has an incomplete specification or no OEM part number.

evidence.note: Estimate; requisition handling continues in scm-purchase-materials.

steps.name: Wait for parts to arrive
steps.description: The work order sits in the backlog with status waiting for material while purchasing sources the part and the supplier ships it. The planner sees the receipt in the ERP when stores post the goods receipt.

evidence.note: Supply chain disruption is a named risk in the 2021 AIF; the wait range (2 to 90 days, mode 14) is the author's estimate for MRO and OEM spares.

steps.name: Mark order ready to schedule
steps.description: When all parts are in stock or reserved, the planner changes the order status to ready, checks the plan hours, and sends a kitting request so stores can pick and stage the parts for the scheduled day.

error.defect_description: Order marked ready while a part is still short.

evidence.note: Estimate of common ERP status practice.

steps.name: Build weekly schedule with operations
steps.description: Each Thursday the planner loads ready orders into the next week's schedule against craft hours available, then agrees it with the operations shift supervisor so that equipment can be released. Jobs that need the unit offline or derated are held for an outage or low-load window.

error.defect_description: Two jobs needing conflicting isolations scheduled on the same day.

next.condition: equipment can be released while the unit runs
needs a unit outage or low-load window

evidence.note: Weekly scheduling is the scheduling practice described by Palmer; share needing an outage window is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Hold order for an outage window
steps.description: The planner tags the order for the next planned or opportunity outage and reviews it when the unit comes offline or the market desk agrees a derate. Work on the boiler, main steam valves and generator mostly falls here.

evidence.note: Spring and fall outage seasons and forced-outage opportunities; wait of 1 week to 4 months is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve weekly schedule and assign crews
steps.description: The maintenance supervisor reviews the draft schedule, checks overtime, vacations and contractor support, assigns named millwrights and technicians to each job and freezes the schedule for the week.

evidence.note: Estimate of common practice; supervisor time shown per order.

steps.name: Request permit and isolation
steps.description: The day before the job the maintenance supervisor enters a permit request in the permit system, naming the equipment, the work, the crew and the isolation points from the job plan, so operations can prepare the isolations. Break-in jobs are requested by phone and entered at once.

error.defect_description: Permit request omits an isolation point or names the wrong equipment tag.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 ss.212-215 (isolation, verification, personal and group locks) applied through the plant permit-to-work procedure

evidence.note: Work needing hazardous energy control may start only after isolation (s.212); the request feeds gas-issue-work-permits.

steps.name: Collect parts kit from stores
steps.description: The lead millwright drives a service truck to the warehouse, signs for the staged kit and any free-issue consumables, checks the parts against the work order, and takes them and the tools to the job.

evidence.note: Estimate; Keephills and Sundance warehouses are some distance from the turbine halls.

steps.name: Sign onto permit and lock on
steps.description: The millwright crew attends the pre-job briefing at the permit desk, reads the permit and isolation list, adds personal locks to the group lock box and tries the start button or checks gauges to confirm the equipment is dead before touching it.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 ss.212-215 (isolation, verification, personal and group locks) applied through the plant permit-to-work procedure

evidence.note: Personal locks and verification (ss.213, 214.1, 215(4)); wait covers the permit queue, which lengthens in outage seasons (author's estimate).

steps.name: Carry out mechanical work
steps.description: Millwrights do the repair or PM task: dismantle, inspect, replace bearings, seals or packing, align and reassemble, following the job plan and OEM manuals. Time is person-minutes for the crew (usually two). If the scope grows or a part is wrong, the order goes back to planning.

error.defect_description: Workmanship defect such as misalignment or a missed fastener.

next.condition: extra parts or scope found, back to planning
needs a crane lift or specialist crew

evidence.note: Wrench time of 35 to 55 percent (Palmer, via reliamag) is why hands-on minutes are far below shift length; job durations are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Collect parts, sign on and lock on (I&E)
steps.description: The instrument and electrical technician collects the staged parts and test equipment, attends the permit briefing, adds a personal lock and proves the circuit dead with a tester before starting.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 ss.212-215 (isolation, verification, personal and group locks) applied through the plant permit-to-work procedure

evidence.note: Personal locks and verification (ss.213, 214.1); minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Carry out instrument or electrical work
steps.description: The technician replaces or calibrates transmitters, positioners, analysers, motor starters or protection relays, checks loop readings against the DCS with the control room, and notes as-found and as-left values.

next.condition: extra parts or scope found, back to planning

evidence.note: Estimate of instrument and electrical job durations.

steps.name: Post-maintenance test with operations
steps.description: After the crew signs off the permit, a field operator restores the equipment and runs it, checking vibration, temperatures, leaks and DCS readings. A failed test sends the job back to the crew.

evidence.note: Estimate; the field operator works rotating shifts so the wait is short.

steps.name: Arrange crane lift or specialist crew
steps.description: The maintenance supervisor asks the outage group for a specialist crew or a crane operator, agrees the date and writes or requests a lift plan for heavy components such as pump casings or fan motors.

evidence.note: Estimate; specialist crews belong to eng-dispatch-specialist-crews.

steps.name: Rig and lift with the turbine hall crane
steps.description: Millwrights and the specialist crew rig the load, hold a lift meeting, and move the component with the turbine hall crane under the lift plan. The crane is tied up for rigging, the lift and landing.

control.basis: Critical lift plan and pre-lift meeting under the plant lifting procedure

evidence.note: Estimate; the crane is shared with outage work, so jobs wait days for it.

steps.name: Review completed order and approve hours
steps.description: The maintenance supervisor reads the crew's notes, checks the hours booked in timekeeping against the plan, and passes the order to the planner for close-out, or sends it back when the notes are missing or unclear.

evidence.note: Estimate of common close-out practice.

steps.name: Key completion data and close the order
steps.description: The planner types the crew's notes, failure codes, actual parts and measurements into the ERP, updates the equipment history and technically completes the order. History feeds reliability analysis.

error.defect_description: Failure codes left blank or generic, weakening reliability analysis.

evidence.note: Estimate; poor failure coding is a common complaint of reliability engineers.

steps.name: Add missing notes or hours
steps.description: The millwright or technician who did the job is found on the next shift, writes the missing as-found condition, parts used or hours on the order, and returns it to the supervisor.

evidence.note: Estimate.

steps.name: Raise follow-up notification
steps.description: Where the crew found further defects that were not fixed, the planner raises a new notification for the deferred work, linked to the closed order, so it enters screening as a new case.

evidence.note: Estimate.

exceptions.name: Parts not in stock
exceptions.description: Non-stock or short parts are requisitioned and the order waits in the backlog for delivery.

exceptions.name: Outage-dependent job
exceptions.description: The equipment cannot be released while the unit runs, so the order waits for a planned or forced outage.

exceptions.name: Priority 1 break-in
exceptions.description: An urgent defect skips planning and scheduling and goes straight to a permit and a crew.

exceptions.name: Scope growth
exceptions.description: The crew finds extra damage or the wrong part, and the order goes back to planning for parts.

exceptions.name: Crane or specialist needed
exceptions.description: Heavy components need the turbine hall crane and a specialist crew, which are shared with outage work.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from PM call or notification to technical completion
benchmarks.population: Routine work orders at a thermal generating plant, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: PM orders are usually done within their one- to two-week window, corrective orders wait in a backlog of several weeks, and parts or outage waits form the long tail. No published cycle-time figure for generator work orders was found.
Base recommendation; the organisation file implies about 5.

benchmarks.unit: share of paid craft time spent on hands-on work

evidence.note: Illustrative figures, not a survey.

pain_points.description: Orders wait for parts that were not stocked or whose stock record was wrong, and planners stop planning to chase them.
Outage-dependent work accumulates between outage seasons and then floods planners, permits and stores in spring and fall.

evidence.note: Common thermal plant pattern; organisation file surge.

pain_points.description: Crews wait at the permit desk in the morning because operators issue permits one at a time.

evidence.note: Common practice; see gen-gas-issue-work-permits.

pain_points.description: Completion notes and failure codes are thin, so equipment history is hard to use for reliability analysis.

evidence.note: Common complaint in plant maintenance; estimate.

sources.title: What is the right ratio of planners to craftspersons for my manufacturing plant?
sources.supports: One planner per 20 to 30 craftspersons as the base recommendation, assuming about 30 percent of pre-planned work is preventive maintenance needing little planner attention; tighter ratios of 1:5 to 1:15 still beneficial; good companies still have a fair amount of reactive work.

sources.title: Maintenance staffing ratios: planner, supervisor, and technician benchmarks
sources.supports: Undated guide. Planner-to-craft 1:20 to 1:30 (Palmer); supervisor span commonly cited as 1:10 to 1:20 with no accepted maintenance-specific target; wrench time raised from 35 to 55 percent by planning and scheduling as Palmer's illustrative example; states these ranges are not SMRP targets.

sources.title: Reliability vs the capricious MRO storeroom
sources.supports: Undated practitioner article on typical MRO storerooms: fill rates of stocked SKUs under 80 percent (out of stock 20 percent of the time); only 50 to 70 percent of planned work orders are filled from stores and 30 to 50 percent cause reactive, emergency purchases; inaccurate inventory quantities disrupt reservations; planners, purchasing and engineers stop their work to chase parts.

sources.title: Occupational Health and Safety Code, Part 15: Managing the Control of Hazardous Energy (consolidated text)
sources.supports: s.212 equipment must be stopped and energy isolated with secured energy-isolating devices before work; s.213 worker tests and confirms the equipment is inoperative before starting; s.214 personal locks with unique identification and a written list of lock holders; s.214.1 each worker secures with own lock, control handed to a supervisor at shift change or reassignment; s.215 group control: supervisor or designated worker secures devices and keys, verifies isolation and posts a report at the work site, each worker locks onto the key-securing system; s.215.1 complex group control procedures certified by a professional engineer, including a work permit or master tag system and separate activation and verification roles; s.215.3 locks removed only by the worker who placed them or a designated supervisor, and only once each worker is accounted for. The text opened is the current consolidation (amended in 2023); the 2019-2022 text had the same section structure.

sources.title: TransAlta Corporation Annual Information Form for the year ended December 31, 2021 (Exhibit 13.1 to Form 40-F)
sources.publisher: TransAlta Corporation via U.S. SEC EDGAR
sources.supports: Forward-looking risk list names disruptions to supply chains, including the ability to secure necessary equipment, and equipment failure and the ability to complete repairs cost-effectively; the partner (Heartland) operates and maintains the Sheerness units; Sundance 4 stopped firing coal from January 1, 2022; Highvale mining ended at the end of 2021; many employees have more than 20 years of service.

assumptions: touch_min for craft steps counts person-minutes for the whole crew, so a two-person job of two hours is 240.

Volume is set at 1,400 orders a month rather than the organisation file's 2,000 because 60 plant crafts cannot deliver 2,000 orders at the hands-on times here; if contractors did a large share of routine work, the higher figure could hold, but contractors are not in the process roles.

Permit preparation, isolation and return are counted in gen-gas-issue-work-permits. Steps s15 and s17 here are the crew's sign-on, the same activity as s12 there; a whole-organisation model should count it once.

The converted gas unit resource is not tied up by routine work: jobs that need the unit offline wait for an outage at s11, and the outage itself belongs to eng-execute-major-outage or gas-respond-forced-outage.
Specialist crew and crane waits (s20, s21) are counted here; the crew's own labour belongs to eng-dispatch-specialist-crews except the millwrights' rigging time.
Incident reports are produced by a very small share of orders (well under 1 percent) and are not modelled as a branch.
Partner-operated Sheerness units are maintained by the partner (aif2021) and are outside this workflow.
Waits for office-hours roles (planner, supervisor) include nights and weekends.
